title: Plan and execute grains and oilseeds sampling and grading processes

lessons.title: Planning the intake sampling and grading process
lessons.html:
Planning before harvest season

At a silo or grain intake point, harvest season brings long queues of trucks from early morning to late evening. A grading process that is not planned leads to delays, mistakes and disputes. As an analyst you plan your station so that every load is sampled and graded correctly and quickly.

Planning checklist

  • Regulations: current grading regulations for each crop expected (white and yellow maize, wheat, sunflower, soybeans, sorghum and others) under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990.
  • Equipment: probes, dividers, sieves of the correct sizes, balances, moisture meters, hectolitre mass apparatus, sample containers and labels.
  • Calibration: balances checked with reference masses, moisture meters checked against reference samples or calibration certificates, sieves inspected for damage.
  • Forms and systems: grading certificates or electronic system working, printer and backup forms ready.
  • Staff: roster for peak hours, trained graders, a supervisor for disputes.
  • Safety: platforms, fall protection, traffic control, dust masks, hearing protection near machinery.

Workflow design

  1. Truck arrives and is weighed on the weighbridge.
  2. Truck is directed to the sampling point.
  3. Sample is taken by probe at the prescribed points.
  4. Sample is reduced and graded in the laboratory.
  5. Grade is captured and the truck directed to the correct bin or rejected.
  6. Reference sample is retained as required.

Plan the layout so samples move quickly and cannot be mixed up: one sample container per truck, labelled at the probe, never left unlabelled on a bench.

Segregation planning

The grade decides where grain is stored. Agree with the silo manager which bins receive which grades and classes, so that high-grade grain is not contaminated by lower grades or by grain with insects or off-odours.

lessons.title: Executing sampling and grading
lessons.html:
Sampling the load

  • Confirm truck identity and delivery documents.
  • Probe at the number of points and pattern required for the vehicle type, reaching the full depth.
  • Combine probe portions, reduce with a divider and fill the labelled container.
  • Note anything abnormal: heat, smell, live insects, wet patches, visible contamination.

Never stand on a load while it is being tipped, never enter a bin, and keep clear of moving trucks.

Grading the sample

  1. Determine moisture with the calibrated meter, following the instrument instructions for the crop.
  2. Weigh the working sample accurately.
  3. Sieve with the prescribed sieve and action, collecting screenings.
  4. Hand-sort the specified portion into the fractions required: foreign matter, other grain, and the defective kernel categories for that crop.
  5. Weigh each fraction and calculate percentages.
  6. Do crop-specific tests, such as hectolitre mass and falling number for wheat.
  7. Compare results with grade limits and assign the class and grade.

Worked calculation

A working sample weighs 250 g. Defective kernels weigh 9.5 g. Percentage defective = 9.5 / 250 x 100 = 3.8%. Compare this figure with the limit in the regulation for each grade. Example figures are illustrative.

Recording and communicating

Record all results, the grade and your name. Give the driver the grading certificate as the procedure requires. If a load is downgraded or rejected, explain the reason using the results.

Disputes

If a producer disputes a grade, follow the site's dispute procedure: the retained reference sample may be regraded by a supervisor or sent to an independent laboratory. Never alter results under pressure.

Quality control during the day

  • Check balances and meters at set intervals.
  • Regrade a percentage of samples blind to check consistency between graders.
  • Clean sieves and benches between samples to avoid carry-over.

Key points

  • Prepare regulations, calibrated equipment, staff and safety before the season.
  • Design a workflow where samples cannot be mixed up.
  • Sample to the full depth at prescribed points and reduce with a divider.
  • Calculate fractions accurately against the correct sample mass.
  • Retain reference samples and follow the dispute procedure.
